You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Diagnosis:
The failed test case "testCoreFunctions" in org.apache.commons.jxpath.ri.compiler.CoreFunctionTest includes assertions that check how core rounding functions (round, floor, ceiling) handle special floating-point values such as NaN (Not a Number) and infinity (positive and negative). The test expects these functions to correctly return Double.NaN when given "NaN" and Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY or Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY when given expressions involving division by zero.

The current bug report explicitly states that core rounding functions do not handle NaN or infinite values correctly, referencing the same test assertions for floor and ceiling and also round("NaN"). This implies the code underlying these functions does not properly cover or return expected values for these special cases.

Attempts to retrieve the code snippets for the invoke methods of rounding-related functions (round, floor, ceiling) showed multiple ambiguities between classes implementing a generic invoke method. This might indicate that the functions are implemented via separate classes or share the same method name but with overloaded or different implementations.

Nevertheless, the root cause likely involves these function implementations not correctly processing special floating-point values:
- NaN inputs might not produce a NaN output,
- divisions by zero might not result in recognized positive or negative infinity outputs,
- so the result is either wrong or not as asserted in the test case.

This could be due to using standard Math.round/floor/ceiling methods without explicit handling of edge cases involving NaN and infinity, or improper conversions that lose these special values.

The recent bug reports do not substantially add useful evidence. One report about incorrect NaN comparisons hints that equality checks or conditional logic on NaN values may be flawed, supporting the idea that special cases are not properly addressed in the core functions.

In summary, the failure originates from missing or incorrect handling of special floating-point values (NaN, +/-Infinity) in the core rounding function implementations invoked by the testCoreFunctions test.

Next, the best course is to inspect the actual implementations of the core rounding functions (round, floor, ceiling) in the org.apache.commons.jxpath.ri.compiler.functions package or equivalent and verify how NaN and infinite values are handled there, fixing the functions to explicitly return expected Double.NaN or infinities when the input corresponds to those values.

Suggested methods to check for fixing: round, floor, and ceiling function invoke methods that take ExpressionContext and Object[] as parameters.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
